fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry — the doctor’s diagnosis of the human condition, the sovereign grace of God, justification and union with Christ, the Christian character of the Sermon on the Mount, the cure of spiritual depression, preaching as logic on fire, and the longing for revival. Seventeen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion to Lloyd-Jones’s ministry, naming his books for the reader’s own further study.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Martyn Lloyd-Jones, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in seventeen short chapters the teaching for which the Welsh physician who became the minister of Westminster Chapel is chiefly remembered — the diagnosis of man’s true condition, the sovereign mercy of God, justification by faith and union with Christ, the Christian character of the Sermon on the Mount, the cure of spiritual depression, the recovery of preaching, the work of the Holy Spirit and the longing for revival — together with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any organisation that holds rights in the writings of Martyn Lloyd-Jones. All descriptions of his teaching are the present author’s own summaries; his books and spoken ministry are named only for the reader’s further study, and readers are warmly encouraged to obtain those works from their rightful publishers. Nothing of Lloyd-Jones’s own text is reproduced here — only Scripture, quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and Ochorus’s account of what he taught.

Lloyd-Jones spent his life turning attention away from the preacher and towards the Word and the Spirit. The right response to his ministry is therefore not admiration of the Doctor but submission to the diagnosis, and flight to the only cure he ever trusted. This volume weighs honestly the places where he was disputed, and ends each chapter where every true sermon should end: with the hearer before God.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:2

In the late 1920s a young London physician, already marked out as one of the ablest men of his generation, gave up medicine to become the minister of a small mission church among the dockers and steelworkers of South Wales. His colleagues thought he had thrown his life away. He spent the next fifty years explaining, in one way or another, why he had not. A physician, he came to believe, can relieve a man’s symptoms and send him home. He cannot touch the thing that is really wrong with him. And the thing that is really wrong with every one of us is not in the body at all.

That man was David Martyn Lloyd-Jones, known for the rest of his life simply as the Doctor. For thirty years he preached at Westminster Chapel in London, a short walk from Buckingham Palace, working his way through books of the Bible verse by verse, sometimes for years at a time. His sermons, gathered after his death into dozens of volumes, are still read on every continent. He did more than any other single figure to recover expository preaching and the theology of the Reformers and the Puritans for the English-speaking evangelical world of the twentieth century.

The one thread

He preached on a great many subjects, but beneath them all ran a single conviction, and it came from the consulting room. The first duty of a physician is diagnosis. Until you know what is wrong, you cannot help; and the commonest failure in medicine, as he had learned at the side of one of the great diagnosticians of the age, is to treat the symptom and miss the disease. Lloyd-Jones carried that conviction into the pulpit and never laid it down. The modern world, he believed, was forever treating symptoms. It thought man’s trouble was ignorance, and offered education. It thought the trouble was poverty, and offered prosperity. It thought the trouble was war, and offered conferences. The church, too often, followed suit, offering entertainment to the bored, therapy to the anxious and activity to the aimless.

The Bible, he insisted, gives a different diagnosis. Man is a sinner, in rebellion against God, under His righteous wrath and unable to save himself. Only when that diagnosis has been accepted does the remedy become good news: that God, who is rich in mercy, has done in Christ what we could never do. That is the thread of this book. The doctor’s diagnosis, and the one cure — it runs through his treatment of the plight of man and the sovereignty of God, through justification and union with Christ, through the Sermon on the Mount and the care of depressed Christians, through his view of preaching and his longing for revival.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, seventeen short chapters take up his key teachings in a rough order. The first group concerns the gospel itself: the diagnosis, the plight of man, the sovereignty of God, the authority of Scripture, justification, the cross and union with Christ. The second concerns the Christian life: the character drawn in the Beatitudes, the Christian as salt and light, the Christian and the world, spiritual depression and its cure, and the working out of salvation. The third concerns the Spirit and the church: the baptism with the Spirit and assurance, revival, preaching, and the church and evangelical unity.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. That is not a decoration. Lloyd-Jones held that preaching which leaves a man merely informed has failed; truth is meant to be applied to the conscience and obeyed. A chapter of this book that is read with interest and changes nothing has missed its purpose. Read slowly. Stop at the questions. Pray.

A word about his words

Lloyd-Jones died in 1981, and his books are not in the public domain. This volume therefore quotes none of his words. Everything said here about his teaching is Ochorus’s own summary, and his books are named throughout so that the reader may go to them. A number of his sermons can be read on Ochorus, and they are the best place to hear his own voice; but the reader who wants the man himself must go to his published works, and should. Nothing here is a substitute. It is, at most, a door.

Reading him with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and he would have disliked one. There are places where he must be read with care, and they will be set out plainly as they arise.

He was a controversial figure in his own lifetime, and the sharpest controversy was his public call in 1966 for evangelicals to leave doctrinally mixed denominations and come together. Many who loved him believed it was a mistake, and it opened a lasting breach with John Stott and a great many Anglican evangelicals. That story is told in chapter nineteen as fairly as we can tell it.

His teaching on the baptism with the Holy Spirit — that it is an experience of assurance and power distinct from conversion, which a believer may lack — was disputed by some of his closest Reformed friends, and is still disputed. It is treated in chapter sixteen, with the objections.

His sermon series were long, and his manner could be severe. He could seem to his critics to despise every method but his own, and his distrust of evangelistic technique and of much in modern church life was at times sweeping. Readers will not always agree with him on what he opposed. They will find it hard to disagree with what he preached.

The counsel of this book is therefore the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Weigh every chapter against the Word of God, which is what he asked of his own hearers every Sunday.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Why listen now

There is a reason his influence has outlived him. He did not chase the questions of his decade. He dealt, as a good physician does, with what does not change: the human heart, its guilt, its fears, its self-deceptions, and its need of God. Fashions in church life have come and gone many times since he stopped preaching. The heart he diagnosed has not changed at all. That is why the patient still needs the Doctor, and why the Doctor would insist, every time, that the patient needs Another far more.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly what you think is the deepest trouble in your own life. Is your answer a symptom or the disease?

2. Consider whether your church life has drifted towards treating symptoms — offering comfort, activity or entertainment where the gospel is needed.

3. Choose a time each week to read one chapter of this book slowly, with a Bible open beside it.

4. Before you begin, name one area where you expect to disagree with Lloyd-Jones, and resolve to test it by Scripture rather than by preference.

5. Read one of his sermons in the Ochorus library this week, and notice how he moves from diagnosis to remedy.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You know what is really wrong with me better than I do. I have been content to treat the symptoms of my life and to leave the disease untouched.
Give me an honest heart as I read. Search me, show me my true condition, and do not let me look away.
And when You have shown me my need, show me Christ, who is the only cure, and make me glad to go to Him. Amen.

fields.title: The Doctor Changes Patients
fields.body_html:
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. PHILIPPIANS 3:7

A Welsh boyhood. David Martyn Lloyd-Jones was born in Cardiff on the twentieth of December, 1899, the second of three sons of Henry Lloyd-Jones, a grocer, and his wife Magdalene. When he was six the family moved to Llangeitho, a village in rural Cardiganshire, where his father kept the shop. It was deep Welsh-speaking country, and it was holy ground in the memory of Welsh Christianity: Llangeitho was where Daniel Rowland had ministered, one of the great preachers of the eighteenth-century awakening, when crowds came from all over Wales to hear him. The boy grew up in the Calvinistic Methodist chapel, which by then was respectable, orderly and, as he later judged it, largely without life. He was clever, argumentative and ambitious. He went on to the county school at Tregaron.

A dairy in Westminster. His father’s business did not prosper, and in 1914 the family left Wales for London, where they ran a dairy business in Westminster. The move put the teenage Martyn within reach of the best education in the country. From Marylebone Grammar School he went, remarkably young, to St Bartholomew’s Hospital Medical School — Bart’s, one of the great teaching hospitals of Britain. On Sundays the family worshipped at the Welsh Presbyterian chapel at Charing Cross. There he came to know Bethan Phillips, whose family came from Newcastle Emlyn in west Wales, and who became a medical student herself, whom he would afterwards marry. Her grandfather, Evan Phillips, had been a preacher of the Welsh revivals.

The chief’s assistant. At Bart’s he was brilliant. He qualified with distinction, took his doctorate in medicine for research on heart disease, and became a Member of the Royal College of Physicians while still in his twenties. Above all, he became chief clinical assistant to Sir Thomas Horder, later Lord Horder, physician to the King and one of the most celebrated diagnosticians of his day. From Horder he learned a method he never forgot: take the history carefully, ask the right questions, refuse to be satisfied by the presenting complaint, reason from the evidence to the cause. A distinguished career lay open before him. He was widely expected to inherit his master’s mantle.

The diagnosis turns. It was during those years that the diagnostician found himself diagnosed. There was no single dramatic moment. Over a period of some two years in the mid-1920s he came under deep conviction of sin, and to a settled faith in Christ as Saviour. With the faith came a disturbing observation. The patients who came to Horder’s rooms, many of them wealthy and distinguished, were very often not ill in body at all, or not only so. Their deepest trouble was guilt, fear, emptiness, the misuse of their lives. He could treat their symptoms and send them away. He could not touch the disease. He became convinced that the most urgent need of men and women was not medical but spiritual, and that he was called to preach.

Sandfields. The decision astonished London. In January 1927 he married Bethan, and that year the two young doctors went to Aberavon, near Port Talbot, where he became minister of the Bethlehem Forward Movement Mission Church at Sandfields, a home-mission work of the Presbyterian Church of Wales among the industrial working class. He had no theological college training. He was ordained, and stayed eleven years. He abolished much that he thought mere machinery, preached the gospel plainly and searchingly, and waited on God. Men and women whom respectable religion had given up on were converted and their lives visibly changed — drinkers, dockers, the hard and the hopeless. Bethan Lloyd-Jones later wrote her own account of those years, Memories of Sandfields. The work gave him an unshakeable confidence that the gospel reaches what nothing else can reach. Their two daughters, Elizabeth and Ann, were born to them.

Westminster Chapel. In 1938 he was called to Westminster Chapel in London, at first to share the pulpit with the veteran expositor G. Campbell Morgan. On Morgan’s retirement in 1943 he became sole minister, and he remained there until 1968. Those were not easy years to begin a London ministry. The war scattered the congregation, and a flying bomb fell nearby in 1944. But he did one essentially unfashionable thing, week after week, for thirty years: he preached consecutively through books of the Bible. The great series became landmarks — the Sermon on the Mount; the Friday-evening exposition of Romans, which ran for some thirteen years; the Sunday-morning series on Ephesians; the sermons on spiritual depression; and many more. Congregations of well over a thousand gathered to hear a man speak, without anecdotes or humour or visual aids, for the better part of an hour.

A wider influence. His work reached far beyond his own pulpit. He was a leading figure among students through the Inter-Varsity Fellowship and served as the first chairman of the International Fellowship of Evangelical Students. With J. I. Packer he began the Puritan Conference in 1950, which did much to bring the Puritans back into evangelical reading. He encouraged the young Banner of Truth Trust, which reprinted older Reformed works. He led a monthly fellowship of ministers for many years, and gave himself freely to pastors and individuals who brought him their troubles. Many came to him in private with problems of every kind, and he would listen and question as he had once done in a consulting room.

A costly disagreement. In October 1966, at the National Assembly of Evangelicals in London, he made a public appeal for evangelicals to come together and to consider leaving denominations that tolerated the denial of the gospel. John Stott, who was in the chair, publicly disagreed. The breach that followed divided British evangelicalism for a generation. It is one of the sorrows of the story, and it is told more fully in chapter nineteen.

The last years. In 1968 he underwent major surgery for cancer, and decided that the time had come to leave Westminster Chapel. His retirement was not idle. He edited his sermons for publication, preached widely, and in 1969 gave the lectures at Westminster Theological Seminary in Philadelphia that became Preaching and Preachers. The flow of books that began then has not stopped since. He preached for the last time in 1980, and his health declined as the cancer returned. He asked his family not to pray for his recovery. He died in his sleep at his home in Ealing on the first of March, 1981 — St David’s Day, the feast of the patron saint of Wales — and was buried at Newcastle Emlyn, in the west Wales country from which his wife’s family had come.

The Doctor. He is remembered by the name everyone gave him, long after he had ceased to practise medicine. It told the truth about him. He had never stopped being a physician. He had only changed his patients, and the disease he treated, and the remedy he prescribed.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Lloyd-Jones gave up a brilliant career because he had seen what was really wrong with people. What have you counted gain that Christ may be asking you to count loss?

2. Consider the patients in Horder’s rooms who were sick in soul rather than body. Is there any symptom in your own life that you have been treating while ignoring its cause?

3. The Sandfields years were built on plain preaching and waiting on God. What machinery in your own service might you lay down in order to trust God more?

4. Pray this week for your own minister, that the Word he preaches may reach the disease and not merely the symptoms.

5. Read a sermon by Lloyd-Jones in the Ochorus library, and notice how often he asks questions of his hearers.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, Great Physician, You saw what was wrong with a young doctor and called him to spend his life on what matters most.
Show me what I am holding on to that You would have me count as loss. Give me courage to lay it down.
Thank You for faithful ministers who preach Your Word plainly. Bless them, keep them, and use them in my life.
And when my own last days come, let me go to You without fear, because my trust is in You alone. Amen.

fields.title: What Is Really Wrong
fields.body_html:
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9

If you want to understand Martyn Lloyd-Jones, begin in a consulting room. A patient comes in complaining of a pain. An inexperienced doctor treats the pain. He prescribes something to dull it, the patient feels better, and both go away satisfied. A great physician does something else. He takes the history. He asks question after question. He examines. He reasons from the symptom to its cause, and he will not prescribe until he knows what is really wrong. Sometimes the pain the patient complains of is the least important thing about him. Sometimes the thing that will kill him is something he has not mentioned at all.

Lloyd-Jones learned that method at the side of Sir Thomas Horder, and he brought it, entire, into the pulpit. It shaped the way he read the Bible, the way he preached, and the way he counselled the troubled men and women who came to his vestry. More than any doctrine, it is the key to his whole ministry.

Symptoms and disease

His great complaint against the modern world, and against much of the modern church, was that it treated symptoms. He preached through the middle decades of a century that had expected to be the most enlightened in history and had instead produced two world wars, the concentration camps and the threat of nuclear annihilation. fields.title: The Plight of Man
fields.body_html:
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins. EPHESIANS 2:1

On Sunday mornings through much of the 1950s and into the 1960s, Lloyd-Jones preached his way through the Epistle to the Ephesians. When he came to the second chapter he lingered over its first three verses for a long time, and the sermons were afterwards published in the volume God’s Way of Reconciliation. One of them, on the wrath of God, can be read on Ochorus. They are among the most searching things he ever preached, and they give his doctrine of man in its fullest form. If the previous chapter showed the doctor’s method, this one shows his diagnosis.

Dead, not ill

Paul’s first word about man without Christ is not that he is sick but that he is dead. Lloyd-Jones pressed the point hard. Much modern preaching, he argued in effect, treats the unbeliever as a man who is ailing but able to help himself: he needs only encouragement, information, a good example, a little assistance. But a dead man cannot be encouraged. He cannot be helped to walk. He must be raised.

And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses. COLOSSIANS 2:13

Spiritual death, as he expounded it, does not mean that the unbeliever is incapable of thought or morality or kindness. It means that he is dead towards God. He has no spiritual life, no true knowledge of God, no love for Him, no capacity of his own to respond to Him. He may be learned, cultured, respectable and religious, and still be dead in this sense. That was the point Lloyd-Jones was most anxious his congregation should grasp, for many of them were learned, cultured, respectable and religious.

Walking according to the course of this world

Paul goes on to describe how such a man lives. He walks according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind.

Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience. EPHESIANS 2:2

Lloyd-Jones saw in this a devastating account of what men call freedom. The unbeliever thinks of himself as independent, thinking his own thoughts, living his own life. In fact, he lives exactly as the world around him lives; his opinions are the opinions of his age; his desires are directed by forces he does not see. He is not free. He is a prisoner who has never noticed the walls. And behind the course of this world stands a personal power of evil, the devil, whose work the Bible takes with complete seriousness even when modern men do not.

Notice too that Paul includes the desires of the mind as well as of the flesh. Sin is not only a matter of the body’s appetites. The proud intellect that sets itself above God is as much in bondage as the drunkard, and perhaps more, because it does not know it.

By nature the children of wrath

Then comes the phrase that most offends the modern ear.

Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. EPHESIANS 2:3

Lloyd-Jones did not soften it. In the sermon on the wrath of God he gives several reasons for facing it squarely. It is in Scripture, and we may not pick and choose. It is a matter of fact, not theory; if it is true, it is the most important fact about every one of us. And, above all, we cannot understand the love of God without it. Why did the Son of God have to come into the world? Why did He have to die? No one, he argued, can answer those questions adequately without the doctrine of the wrath of God. Take away the wrath and the cross becomes an unexplained tragedy, or a mere example.

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness. ROMANS 1:18

He was careful to say what wrath is not. It is not a loss of temper, not a sudden outburst of irritation, not the capricious anger of a pagan deity. It is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of God to all that is evil — the reaction of perfect holiness to sin. A God who was not angry with evil would not be good.

And note the words even as others. Paul, the converted Pharisee, includes himself. There is no class of person exempt. The religious and the irreligious, the moral and the immoral, the Jew and the Gentile, all alike are by nature under the wrath of God. This is what the Bible means by the universality of sin, and it is the great leveller of human pride.

For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God. ROMANS 3:23

Why begin here

A reader may ask why a preacher would spend so long on such dark matters. Lloyd-Jones’s answer was always the same, and it was the answer of a physician. You do not understand the cure until you understand the disease. The man who thinks he is only slightly unwell will not value the surgeon. The man who knows he is dying will value him above everything.

This is why he was so critical of any presentation of the gospel that began with man’s happiness, or his needs, or his potential, rather than with his condition before God. Such preaching, he believed, produced shallow conversions, because it offered Christ as an addition to a life that was basically sound, rather than as the only hope of a life that was lost.

And then the great But

Yet his exposition never ended in darkness, and it would be a serious misreading of him to think it did. The whole purpose of Ephesians 2:1–3 is to prepare for verse four. The sermon on the wrath of God closes by turning, with evident joy, to the glorious But that follows.

But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) EPHESIANS 2:4–5

Lloyd-Jones loved those two words, But God. They were, for him, the whole gospel in miniature. Man’s condition is hopeless — but God. Man is dead — but God has made alive. Man is under wrath — but God is rich in mercy. The darkness of the diagnosis is there to make the light of the remedy visible. Only the man who has seen the depth of the pit can sing properly of the hand that lifted him out of it.

Where care is needed

This doctrine can be preached badly. It can be used to crush rather than to lead to Christ, or preached with a coldness that suggests the preacher is not himself one of the others. Lloyd-Jones knew this danger, and his own practice was to hold the wrath and the mercy of God together, never one without the other. The reader who takes this chapter to heart should do the same: see your condition truly, and then look immediately and long at the mercy of God in Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Ephesians 2:1–10 aloud. Mark where the description of man ends and the action of God begins.

2. Ask where you have thought of yourself, or others, as merely ill rather than dead towards God. How would the difference change your prayers for unbelieving friends?

3. Consider whether your opinions and desires are truly your own, or simply the course of this world. Name one area where you have followed the age without thinking.

4. If the doctrine of the wrath of God troubles you, write down what you think the cross means without it. Then read Romans 3:23–26.

5. Spend five minutes thanking God for the words But God, applying them to your own story.

A PRAYER
Holy God, I confess that by nature I was dead towards You, walking in the way of this world, and a child of wrath even as others.
I do not deserve Your mercy, and I do not ask for it as a right. I cast myself upon it.
Thank You that You are rich in mercy, and that You loved me when I was dead, and made me alive together with Christ.
Let the memory of what I was keep me humble, and the knowledge of what You have done keep me glad. Amen.

fields.title: The Sovereignty of God
fields.body_html:
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

Martyn Lloyd-Jones was a Calvinist, and he said so without embarrassment. But the word can mislead. He was not interested in Calvinism as a party badge or a debating position, and he had little patience with those who were. What gripped him was something larger and older than any system: the living God, who is sovereign over all things and who saves sinners by His own free grace from first to last. That conviction was the backbone of his preaching. Take it away, and the rest of his teaching falls to pieces.

Where the gospel begins

The modern tendency, he believed, was to begin with man — his needs, his feelings, his decision — and to fit God in around him. The Bible begins with God. It begins with His being, His holiness, His purposes, His glory. Lloyd-Jones insisted that the first question of religion is not what man wants but who God is, and that until that question has been answered, every other will be answered wrongly.

O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! ROMANS 11:33

This is why so many of his series began with long expositions of doctrine before they ever came to application. He was not being academic. He was convinced that Christians are made weak by small thoughts of God, and strong by great ones. A man who knows that God is on the throne can face anything. A man who suspects that everything depends on himself will sooner or later break.

Salvation is of the Lord

When Lloyd-Jones spoke of the sovereignty of God, he meant chiefly His sovereignty in salvation. The previous chapter showed his diagnosis: man is dead in trespasses and sins. It follows that man cannot save himself, cannot even contribute to his salvation, cannot of his own resources so much as turn towards God. If he is to be saved at all, God must do it.

No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. JOHN 6:44

And God does do it. He chose His people in Christ before the foundation of the world. He sent His Son to redeem them. He sends His Spirit to give them life, to open their eyes and to draw them to Christ. He keeps them to the end. In his expositions of Ephesians 1 and of Romans 8 and 9, Lloyd-Jones worked through these truths with evident delight. They were not, for him, cold propositions. They were the ground of all assurance and all praise.

According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love. EPHESIANS 1:4

He was quick to point out that election in Scripture is always unto holiness. It is not a licence for complacency. The believer who says, in effect, that since he is chosen it does not matter how he lives has shown by that very statement that he has not understood the doctrine.

Grace that humbles and grace that comforts

Two great fruits of this doctrine appear again and again in his preaching.

fields.title: The Authority of Scripture
fields.body_html:
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. 2 TIMOTHY 3:16

Lloyd-Jones began his ministry in an age when the Bible had lost its authority in most of the churches of Britain. The higher criticism of the nineteenth century had filtered down from the universities into the pulpits, and many ministers no longer believed that Scripture was the Word of God in any sense their grandparents would have recognised. Preaching had become, in many places, a matter of moral uplift, literary appreciation or comment on the events of the day. Against all of this Lloyd-Jones set himself with a single, unwavering conviction: the Bible is the Word of God, and the preacher’s whole business is to expound it.

The question of authority

He believed that the great question facing the church of his day was not evangelism or social action or unity, important as those were, but authority. On what basis does the church speak at all? If it speaks only on the basis of human opinion, it has nothing to say that the world cannot say better. If it speaks on the basis of the Word of God, it has everything to say. In a short book called Authority, published in the late 1950s, he set out the matter under three heads: the authority of Christ, the authority of Scripture and the authority of the Holy Spirit. The three stand together. Christ Himself received the Old Testament as the Word of His Father, and commissioned His apostles to speak in His name; the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures is the Spirit who illumines them.

Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. MATTHEW 24:35

The Christian who takes Christ as Lord, he argued in effect, cannot take a lower view of Scripture than Christ took. The attempt to separate the authority of Jesus from the authority of the Bible fails at the first step, because it is from the Bible that we know Jesus at all, and because Jesus Himself submitted to its authority.

Scripture interprets Scripture

His reverence for the Bible was not blind. It shaped a careful method of reading. In the sermon on the prodigal son hosted on Ochorus, he lays down two principles that he followed everywhere. First, no passage may be interpreted in a way that contradicts the plain teaching of Scripture elsewhere, because the Bible is one revelation from one God, and there are no real contradictions in it, though there are many things we cannot fully understand. Second, one must not build doctrines on what a passage does not say. A parable, for instance, is given to teach one great positive lesson, and it is folly to argue that because the parable of the prodigal son does not mention the cross, the cross is unnecessary.

Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. 2 PETER 1:20–21

He believed that most heresies would never have arisen if these two simple rules had been kept. They are worth any reader’s keeping still.

Expository preaching

His view of Scripture determined his whole approach to preaching. If the Bible is the Word of God, then the preacher’s task is not to find a text to hang his own ideas upon, but to let the text speak. That is why he preached consecutively through whole books, verse by verse. It kept the preacher from riding his hobby-horses. It compelled him to deal with passages he would otherwise have avoided. It taught the congregation to read the Bible for themselves. And it trusted the Word to do its own work.

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. HEBREWS 4:12

He was not interested in exposition as a lecture, however. He was scathing about preachers who gave a running commentary on a passage and never applied it. Exposition, for him, meant taking the doctrine out of the text and pressing it home upon the hearer until he was confronted by God. The Word of God is not a museum piece to be admired. It is a living voice that calls for a response.

The Bible and the modern mind

He was often told that modern men could no longer believe the Bible, and he was unimpressed. In the sermon on the light of the world, he observes that the world has always spoken of its enlightenment, from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century to his own day, and that in spite of all its real advances in knowledge of the natural world, it knows no more than ever about the things that matter most — about God, about the soul, about how to live and how to die. The modern mind, he argued, is not the final court of appeal. The Word of God judges it, not the other way round.

For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:18

This did not make him anti-intellectual. He was a man of formidable learning, and he read widely in history, philosophy and science. But he refused to allow any human learning to sit in judgment on the Word of God. When the two appeared to conflict, he was prepared to wait, confident that it was human learning that would change.

Where care is needed

A high view of Scripture can be held in a way that is harsh or proud, as though holding the right doctrine of the Bible were the same as obeying it. Lloyd-Jones knew the difference, and warned against an orthodoxy that was dead. It is also worth saying that faithful Christians who share his conviction about Scripture have sometimes differed from him about particular interpretations — on prophecy, on the gifts of the Spirit, on church order — and that his own readings, like anyone’s, must be tested by the Word he loved. He would have been the first to insist on it.

Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask honestly what is the final authority in your life: Scripture, your feelings, your church’s traditions, or the opinions of your age.

2. Choose one short book of the Bible and read it through this month, a little each day, from beginning to end.

3. Next time you find a passage you dislike, do not skip it. Ask what it says, why it says it, and what it requires of you.

4. When you hear a sermon, check whether the point of the sermon is the point of the text.

5. Memorise Hebrews 4:12 and pray it before you open your Bible each day this week.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You have spoken, and Your Word is truth. Forgive me for treating it as one voice among many.
Give me a humble mind, willing to be corrected by what You have said rather than correcting it by what I think.
Let Your Word be a lamp to my feet: not a subject I study but a voice I obey.
And raise up preachers who will open the Scriptures faithfully, that Your people may hear You speak. Amen.

fields.title: Justified by Faith
fields.body_html:
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

For some thirteen years, on Friday evenings, Martyn Lloyd-Jones expounded the Epistle to the Romans at Westminster Chapel. He began in 1955 and was still in the fourteenth chapter when illness ended his ministry there in 1968. The sermons, published after his death in fourteen volumes, are perhaps the fullest exposition of the epistle ever preached from an English pulpit. At the centre of them all lies the doctrine he regarded as the heart of the gospel: justification by faith alone.

The question behind all questions

He liked to put it in the form of Job’s ancient question.

How then can man be justified with God? or how can he be clean that is born of a woman? JOB 25:4

That, he insisted, is the most important question a human being can ask. Not how can I be happy, or how can I find meaning, or how can I overcome my problems — but how can I, a sinner, stand before a holy God? Every religion and every philosophy offers some answer. Most of them, in the end, say the same thing: do your best, and hope. The gospel says something utterly different.

What justification is

Lloyd-Jones was careful, as a physician is careful, to define his terms. Justification, he taught, is a legal or forensic word. It does not mean to make a man righteous in his character; that is the work of sanctification, which follows. It means to declare a man righteous in his standing before the law. It is the verdict of the Judge.

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 3:24

How can a holy God declare a sinner righteous without ceasing to be holy? That is the problem Paul raises and answers in Romans 3:21–26, a passage to which Lloyd-Jones devoted an entire volume, Atonement and Justification. The answer is the cross. God set forth His Son as a propitiation — a sacrifice that turns away His own wrath — so that He might be both just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus. Our sins were reckoned to Christ and punished in Him. His righteousness is reckoned to us and received by faith.

To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. ROMANS 3:26

He loved to point out that justification is complete and final. It is not a process, not a gradual improvement, not something that fluctuates from day to day. The believer who trusted Christ this morning is as fully justified as the apostle Paul. The verdict has been given, and it will never be reversed.

Faith is not a work

He guarded carefully against a subtle error. Faith is the instrument by which we receive justification, but it is not the ground of it. We are not justified because of our faith, as if faith were a new kind of good work that God rewards. We are justified through faith, on the ground of Christ’s work alone. Faith contributes nothing; it simply receives. A beggar’s hand does not earn the gift that is placed in it.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. EPHESIANS 2:8

This mattered pastorally. Many anxious Christians, he observed, are forever examining their faith, wondering whether it is strong enough or real enough to save them. They have made faith into a work. The remedy is to stop looking at their faith and look at Christ. It is not the strength of faith that saves, but the strength of the One in whom it rests.

The test of true preaching

One of the best-known points in his exposition of Romans concerns chapter six. Paul, having set out justification by grace in chapter five, immediately anticipates an objection: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?

What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. ROMANS 6:1–2

Lloyd-Jones drew from this a bold conclusion. If Paul’s preaching of justification could be misunderstood in that way, then true preaching of justification will always be liable to the same misunderstanding. If a man’s preaching of the gospel never exposes him to the charge that he is making sin easy, he has probably not preached the gospel of free grace at all; he has preached salvation by works with a little grace added. It is one of his most searching tests, and it has troubled many a preacher since.

He did not, of course, think the objection was right. Paul’s answer is God forbid, and the rest of Romans 6 shows why: the justified man has died with Christ and been raised to new life; he cannot go on living as before. But the doctrine itself must be preached so freely that the objection arises.

Peace with God

The fruit of justification, Paul says, is peace with God. Lloyd-Jones distinguished this from the peace of God, a feeling of calm that may come and go. Peace with God is a state, a settled relationship. The war is over. The enmity is ended. The believer stands in grace.

By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. ROMANS 5:2

His volume on Romans 5, which he called Assurance, dwells on this at length. He was convinced that many Christians live far below their privileges because they have never grasped that their justification is settled. They are still, in their hearts, on trial. They need to hear, again and again, that there is therefore now no condemnation.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:1

Where care is needed

It is possible to hold the doctrine of justification with perfect orthodoxy and to be unchanged by it — to use it as a pillow rather than a foundation. Lloyd-Jones warned against this as sharply as he warned against legalism. Justification is never alone; the one God justifies He also sanctifies. The reader who rejoices in this chapter should read the chapters that follow, on union with Christ and on working out salvation, as its necessary companions.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Answer Job’s question in your own words, in writing, without using any religious jargon.

2. Ask whether you have been treating your faith as a work — examining it anxiously instead of looking to Christ.

3. Read Romans 3:21–26 slowly three times this week. Underline every word that speaks of what God has done.

4. If you are a preacher or teacher, ask whether anyone has ever misunderstood you as making sin easy. What might that tell you?

5. Each morning this week, before anything else, say to yourself: There is therefore now no condemnation. Then live the day in that light.

A PRAYER
Righteous Father, I could never stand before You in my own righteousness. My best works are stained, and my sins are many.
Thank You that You have set forth Your Son as the propitiation for my sins, and that You are just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus.
Take my eyes off my faith, and fix them on Christ. Let me rest in His finished work and in Your final verdict.
And since You have justified me freely, let me never use Your grace as an excuse for sin, but as the reason to live for You. Amen.

Our sins were reckoned to Christ and punished in Him. His righteousness is reckoned to us and received by faith. Answer Job’s question in your own words, in writing, without using any religious jargon. 2. Ask whether you have been treating your faith as a work — examining it anxiously instead of looking to Christ. 3. Read Romans 3:21–26 slowly three times this week. Underline every word that speaks of what God has done. 4. If you are a preacher or teacher, ask whether anyone has ever misunderstood you as making sin easy. What might that tell you? 5. Each morning this week, before anything else, say to yourself: There is therefore now no condemnation. Then live the day in that light. A PRAYER Righteous Father, I could never stand before You in my own righteousness. My best works are stained, and my sins are many. Thank You that You have set forth Your Son as the propitiation for my sins, and that You are just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus. Take my eyes off my faith, and fix them on Christ. Let me rest in His finished work and in Your final verdict. And since You have justified me freely, let me never use Your grace as an excuse for sin, but as the reason to live for You. Amen.

fields.body_html:
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. GALATIANS 6:14

Among the shorter books drawn from Lloyd-Jones’s preaching is a series of sermons on a single verse, Galatians 6:14, published under the plain title The Cross. It is one of the best places to begin reading him. In it the physician turns from diagnosis to remedy, and the remedy is the one thing Paul says he will boast of. Everything Lloyd-Jones taught about sin, wrath and justification converged here. The cross was not one doctrine among many. It was the centre that held them all together.

Why Paul gloried in it

Lloyd-Jones began by noting how strange Paul’s statement is. The cross, in the ancient world, was the most shameful of deaths, reserved for slaves and criminals. No educated man would have mentioned it in polite company. And Paul, a man of learning and pedigree, says it is the only thing he will glory in. Why?

He answered, in effect, that Paul had seen what the cross really was. To the Jew it was a stumbling block and to the Greek foolishness, because both judged it by appearances. Paul judged it by revelation, and saw in it the wisdom and power of God.

But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:23–24

What the cross reveals

Lloyd-Jones was insistent that the cross must be understood, not merely felt. It is possible to be moved by the sufferings of Christ as one is moved by any noble death, and to miss entirely what was happening. The cross is not first a revelation of human cruelty, nor even chiefly an example of self-sacrifice, though it is both. It is God dealing with sin.

He drew out several things the cross reveals. It reveals the true character of the world, which, when God came among it in the person of His Son, took Him and nailed Him to a tree. It reveals the terrible seriousness of sin, which could be dealt with at no smaller cost. It reveals the justice of God, who would not simply overlook sin but punished it in the person of the Substitute. And above all it reveals the love of God, who did not spare His own Son.

He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? ROMANS 8:32

Lloyd-Jones taught what the Reformers and the Puritans taught before him: that Christ died in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty of their sin, and so turned away the wrath of God from them. He believed that every attempt to explain the cross without substitution ends by explaining it away. If Christ did not bear our punishment, why did He have to die at all?

Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. 1 PETER 2:24

The world crucified to me

But Galatians 6:14 does not stop at the cross as the ground of forgiveness. Paul goes on: by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. Lloyd-Jones gave careful attention to these words, because they show that the cross changes not only a man’s standing but his whole outlook.

The man who has truly seen the cross can never look at the world in the same way again. He has seen what the world did to the Son of God. He has seen the world’s wisdom exposed as folly, its values as empty, its judgement as false. The world has lost its power to charm him. And equally, he is crucified to the world: it no longer regards him as one of its own. He has become a stranger in it.

Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:15

This, for Lloyd-Jones, was the real cure for worldliness. Not a list of prohibitions, but a sight of the cross. The Christian who is still captivated by the world has not yet looked at Calvary long enough.

The cross and pride

He also saw the cross as the great destroyer of human pride. At the foot of the cross all distinctions are levelled. The learned and the ignorant, the moral and the immoral, the religious and the profane stand together as sinners who can be saved only by the death of Another. No one can boast there, except in the cross itself.

For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:2

It is worth noticing that this was the note on which he chose to preach, in an age that was increasingly embarrassed by the cross and anxious to present Christianity as a programme of moral and social improvement. He believed that the church which loses the cross has lost its reason for existing. It may still do much good work; it will no longer be able to save anyone.

Where care is needed

The reader should not take from this chapter the idea that the cross is merely a doctrine to be defended. Lloyd-Jones defended it vigorously, but he preached it first of all as a message to be received and a sight to be wondered at. He would also want the reader to see that the doctrine of substitution is not an abstraction. It is personal: He loved me, and gave Himself for me. A cross that is understood but never adored has not yet been understood.

The Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. GALATIANS 2:20
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what you are tempted to glory in: your abilities, your reputation, your family, your service. Name it before God.

2. Spend a quiet half-hour this week reading the account of the crucifixion in one Gospel, asking at every step what it reveals about sin and about God.

3. Explain to a friend, in plain words, why Christ had to die. If you find you cannot, study Romans 3:21–26 and 1 Peter 2:24 until you can.

4. Identify one way in which the world still has a hold on your affections. Set the cross against it in prayer.

5. Sing or read a hymn about the cross slowly, meaning every line.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You bore my sins in Your own body on the tree. You took my place and my punishment. I cannot understand such love; I can only receive it.
Forbid that I should glory in anything but Your cross. Strip away my pride and every false boast.
Let the world be crucified to me, and me to the world, so that its charms have no more power over me.
Keep me always near the cross, wondering, grateful and glad. Amen.

fields.title: In Christ
fields.body_html:
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

If justification was, for Lloyd-Jones, the heart of the gospel, union with Christ was the heart of the Christian life. He returned to it constantly. In his exposition of Romans 6, published as The New Man, he worked through it with great care. In his sermons on Ephesians he found it on almost every page. And in his evangelistic preaching he loved to tell his hearers that believing in Christ is not merely an intellectual matter but a joining — that the believer enters into a real, living union with Christ and begins to share in all that is His. The sermon Full Salvation, which can be read on Ochorus, makes exactly that point.

More than forgiveness

Many Christians, he observed, think of salvation almost entirely in terms of forgiveness. Christ died; my sins are pardoned; I shall go to heaven when I die. All of that is gloriously true. But it is not the whole truth, and a Christian who knows only that much is living far below his privileges. The New Testament’s great phrase for the Christian is not the forgiven man but the man in Christ.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

To be in Christ means that everything that is true of Christ becomes, in a real sense, true of the believer. When Christ died, the believer died with Him. When Christ rose, the believer rose with Him. Christ is seated in the heavenly places, and the believer is seated there in Him. This is not poetry or mere metaphor. It is the plain teaching of Scripture about what has happened to every Christian.

Romans 6: the old man is dead

Lloyd-Jones gave particular attention to Romans 6, because he believed it was widely misunderstood. Paul says that our old man is crucified with Christ.

Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin. ROMANS 6:6

He argued, with characteristic precision, that the old man is not the sinful nature that remains in the believer, but the man we were in Adam — our old self, our old position, our old identity under the reign of sin. That man is dead. He died with Christ. He is never coming back. The Christian is not a divided person with an old man and a new man fighting inside him; he is a new man who still has to contend with sin remaining in his mortal body.

This was not hair-splitting. It had immense practical consequences. The Christian who thinks of his old self as still alive will struggle hopelessly against it. The Christian who knows that his old self died with Christ can reckon on that fact, and resist sin from a position of victory rather than defeat.

Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. ROMANS 6:11

He was careful, too, to insist that this reckoning is not a technique for producing an experience. It is the believer’s acceptance of what God says is already true. The facts come first; the reckoning follows; the experience grows out of both.

All things are yours

He loved the sweep of Paul’s argument in 1 Corinthians 3, where the apostle rebukes the church for boasting in human leaders.

Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:21–23

In the sermon Full Salvation he draws out the implications. Because the believer is Christ’s, all things are his. The apostles and preachers are not his masters but his servants. The great minds of history are not to be trembled before but used. The world itself is not to be feared or worshipped, because it belongs to the believer’s Lord. And beyond all this, there is an inheritance reserved in heaven that the believer shares as a joint heir with Christ.

And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. ROMANS 8:17

This was, for Lloyd-Jones, the answer to the small, anxious, defeated Christianity he saw all around him. Christians live like beggars though they are heirs, because they do not know who they are.

Life in Christ

In the years after the war Lloyd-Jones preached through the First Epistle of John, and the sermons were afterwards gathered under the title Life in Christ. There he showed that union with Christ is not only a status but a fellowship — a daily walking in the light, a daily communion with the Father and the Son.

That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ. 1 JOHN 1:3

He was anxious that believers should not be content with knowing the doctrine of union. They should enjoy it. The New Testament speaks of joy, of assurance, of the love of God shed abroad in the heart. These are not extras for the spiritually advanced. They are the ordinary experience of the man in Christ, and a Christian who lacks them should ask why.

Where care is needed

Lloyd-Jones’s reading of the old man in Romans 6 is not accepted by all good interpreters, and some think he pressed the distinction between the old man and the remaining sinful nature further than the text requires. The reader need not settle that question to receive the main point, which is beyond dispute: the believer has been joined to Christ, has died and risen with Him, and is called to live in the light of that fact. Nor should the reader take union with Christ as a reason to think lightly of remaining sin. The man in Christ is still called to put sin to death daily. He does so not to become united to Christ, but because he already is.

For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. COLOSSIANS 3:3
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Ephesians 1 and 2 and underline every occurrence of the phrases in Christ, in him and with Christ. Count them.

2. Ask whether you think of yourself chiefly as a forgiven sinner or as a man or woman in Christ. What difference would the second make today?

3. When you are next tempted, remind yourself deliberately: my old self died with Christ. I am not what I was.

4. Consider one thing or person that you have been fearing or idolising. Bring 1 Corinthians 3:21–23 to bear on it.

5. Spend time this week not asking God for anything, but simply enjoying fellowship with the Father and the Son.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I thank You that I am not only forgiven but joined to You — that I died with You, rose with You, and am seated with You.
Forgive me for living like a beggar when You have made me an heir. Open my eyes to see who I am in You.
When sin presses upon me, teach me to reckon myself dead to it and alive to God.
And let me not only know this truth but enjoy it, in daily fellowship with the Father and with You. Amen.

fields.title: The Christian Character
fields.body_html:
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:3

Of all Lloyd-Jones’s books, the one most widely read is probably his Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, first preached on Sunday mornings at Westminster Chapel in the early 1950s and published in two volumes at the end of that decade. Several of those sermons can be read on Ochorus. It is a good book to start with, because it shows the Doctor at his most practical, and because its subject is one no Christian can avoid: what a Christian actually is.

For whom was the Sermon preached

He began by clearing away misunderstandings. Others set it aside altogether, arguing that it described the law of a future kingdom and did not apply directly to Christians now. Lloyd-Jones rejected both views.

The Sermon, he argued, is addressed to disciples. It describes the life of those who belong to the kingdom of heaven now. It is not a way of becoming a Christian; it is a description of what a Christian is. And it is not a counsel of perfection for a later age; it is the standard for every believer today. To offer it to the unconverted world as a programme is to mock them, because no one can live it without a new nature. To put it off to the future is to evade its present claim.

Character before conduct

The Beatitudes come first, and Lloyd-Jones insisted that the order matters. Before our Lord says anything about what Christians must do, He describes what they are. Conduct flows from character. The New Testament never asks a man to behave like a Christian before he has become one.

He made several observations about the Beatitudes as a whole. They describe every Christian, not a select few. There is no suggestion that some believers are poor in spirit while others are merciful, as though the qualities were distributed like gifts. All of them belong to every Christian, in some measure. They are not natural temperaments; a man may be naturally easygoing without being meek, or naturally melancholy without mourning for sin. They are the fruit of grace. And they mark the Christian out as essentially different from the man of the world. The world admires the self-confident, the assertive, the strong; our Lord pronounces blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek.

He dwelt longest on the first Beatitude, because he believed it is the key to all the rest. To be poor in spirit is not to be weak, timid or self-deprecating in manner. It is to see oneself truly before God: to have no confidence in one’s own righteousness, gifts, birth or achievements, and to come to God with empty hands.

He believed this was precisely the quality most lacking in the church of his day, which was inclined to advertise its famous converts and to present Christianity as the religion of the successful. Nothing, he held, is further from the spirit of the Sermon. The man who is truly poor in spirit will not be impressed by himself, and will not want others to be impressed by him.

The Beatitudes that follow grow naturally out of the first. The man who sees his poverty mourns over his sin, and over the sin of the world — and it is to such mourners that comfort is promised. And he hungers and thirsts after righteousness. Lloyd-Jones loved this Beatitude, because it carries its own promise. A man who hungers for righteousness — not for happiness, not for experiences, but for righteousness, to be right with God and like Him — will be filled. He believed that many Christians seek blessings and experiences directly and are disappointed, while those who seek holiness find joy as well.

The later Beatitudes turn outward. The man who has received mercy becomes merciful. The pure in heart are those whose whole being is directed towards God, without guile or mixed motives; they shall see God. The peacemakers are not those who avoid trouble at any price, but those who, having been reconciled to God, seek to reconcile others to Him and to one another. And the persecuted — those who suffer for righteousness’ sake — are blessed because such suffering proves that they are different from the world.

Lloyd-Jones was careful to note that the persecution in view is for righteousness’ sake. A Christian who suffers because he is tactless, or aggressive, or self-righteous, may not claim the blessing.

This teaching can be heard as a counsel of despair. Who can be all these things? Lloyd-Jones’s answer was that the Beatitudes are not a ladder to climb in order to be saved, but a description of what God produces in those He saves. They are to be read as a mirror, and then as a promise. It should also be said that his rejection of dispensational readings, though widely shared, is not universal among evangelicals. The reader need not decide that question to feel the Sermon’s searching claim upon his own life now — which was the point Lloyd-Jones cared most about.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Matthew 5:1–12 slowly. Which Beatitude describes you least? Make it the subject of your prayer this week.

2. Ask whether you have been trying to behave like a Christian without first depending on God for a Christian heart.

3. Consider what you are most tempted to be proud of. Bring it to God and confess your poverty of spirit.

4. Notice this week how you respond when you are slighted or misunderstood. Is it meekness, or wounded pride?

5. Ask whether you hunger more for blessings and experiences, or for righteousness. Pray for the second.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You looked upon Your disciples and called them blessed. Make me one of them in truth.
Empty me of self-confidence and make me poor in spirit. Teach me to mourn for my sin and to be meek towards others.
Give me a hunger for righteousness greater than my hunger for comfort or success, and fill me as You have promised.
Make me merciful, pure in heart and a peacemaker, and if I must suffer, let it be for Your sake alone. Amen.

fields.title: Salt and Light
fields.body_html:
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men. MATTHEW 5:13

Having described the Christian character in the Beatitudes, our Lord at once turns to the Christian’s place in the world. Ye are the salt of the earth. Ye are the light of the world. Lloyd-Jones’s sermons on these two verses, both of which can be read on Ochorus, are among his most direct, and they address a question that pressed hard on the church of his day and presses still: what is the relationship between the Christian and the society around him?

Not out of the world

He began by rejecting one answer outright. The Christian life does not mean withdrawal from the world. That, he argued, was the error of monasticism, which taught that true holiness required separation from ordinary society and a life of contemplation behind walls. Our Lord’s words forbid it. Salt that is kept in the cellar preserves nothing. Light hidden under a bushel shines on no one.

I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. JOHN 17:15

The Christian is in the world though not of it. He is to be otherworldly in his mind and outlook, but he is to live out that outlook in the office, the factory, the home and the street. That is where the salt is needed.

What the metaphor says about the world

Lloyd-Jones pointed out that the statement Ye are the salt of the earth is not only a description of the Christian. It is, by implication, a description of the world. Salt was used in the ancient world chiefly to preserve meat from corruption. To call Christians the salt of the earth is to say that the earth, left to itself, is corrupting.

He found in the twentieth century abundant confirmation. He recalled the easy optimism of the thinkers at the end of the nineteenth century, who expected the new century to be a golden age of progress, education and peace; and he set beside it the two world wars and the horrors that followed. The biblical view of the world, he argued, had been vindicated by history. Humanity left to itself does not rise; it decays.

The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. GENESIS 6:11

How salt works

What then does the Christian do? Lloyd-Jones’s answer was characteristically careful. Salt works not by noise but by presence. It does not need to announce itself; it simply is what it is, and its presence checks corruption. So the Christian, by being what he is — by his character, his conduct, his refusal to join in the world’s corruption — acts as a restraint upon the evil around him. His mere presence in a room can change the tone of a conversation.

He applied this pointedly. The great hope for society, he argued, is not a programme of the church but an increasing number of individual Christians, each exercising this preserving influence in his own circle. He appealed to the Methodist revival of the eighteenth century, and the transformation of English society that followed it, as proof that genuine Christians in large numbers change a nation.

When the salt loses its savour

But our Lord adds a warning. Salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing. Lloyd-Jones took this as a solemn word to the church. A Christian who has become like the world has lost the very thing that made him useful. He no longer preserves anything, and he is trodden under foot of men. The world does not respect a worldly Christian; it despises him.

Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. ROMANS 12:2

He saw this as one explanation of the church’s weakness in his day. It had tried to win the world by becoming like it, and had succeeded only in losing its savour.

The light of the world

The second figure goes further than the first. Salt is negative: it prevents corruption. Light is positive: it reveals, guides and illuminates.

Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. MATTHEW 5:14

In the sermon on this verse, Lloyd-Jones dwells on the astonishing fact that our Lord said these words to a crowd of unimportant people from the world’s point of view. Ye — you, and you alone — are the light of the world. The world talks constantly of its own enlightenment, he observed, yet in the things that matter most it remains in gross darkness. Its knowledge of things has multiplied; its knowledge of how to live has not.

The Christian is light because he is joined to Christ, who is the Light of the world. He reflects a light that is not his own. And he shines both by his life and by his word. Lloyd-Jones insisted on both. A Christian who talks but does not live has no light; but a Christian who lives well and never explains why leaves the world admiring him rather than glorifying God.

Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 5:16

He pictured the ideal: a Christian so evidently different — so calm under pressure, so free from the world’s dependence on artificial pleasures, so balanced — that his neighbours are driven to ask what he has. Then he can tell them.

Where care is needed

Lloyd-Jones was wary of the church as an institution becoming absorbed in political and social campaigns, and he believed its first calling was to preach the gospel and make Christians, not to reform society directly. Many evangelicals since have thought he drew that line too sharply, and that Christians have a clearer calling to public justice and mercy than he allowed. The reader may weigh that. But his central point stands untouched: no programme can do what salt and light do, and a church that has lost its savour will change nothing, however busy it is.

Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men. 2 CORINTHIANS 3:2
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of the places where you spend most of your week. Is your presence there felt as salt? What would change if it were?

2. Ask whether you have become so like the world around you that you have lost your savour. Name one specific area.

3. Consider whether your light shines by life alone, by word alone, or by both. Which needs strengthening?

4. Pray this week for one colleague or neighbour by name, and look for a natural opportunity to explain your hope.

5. Read Matthew 5:13–16 each day this week and ask God to make you useful where He has placed you.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You have called me the salt of the earth and the light of the world. I confess that I have often hidden my light and lost my savour.
Keep me in the world but not of it. Let my life be a check on the corruption around me, and my words a light to those in darkness.
Deliver me from conforming to this world. Transform me by the renewing of my mind.
And let those who see my life be drawn not to admire me, but to glorify my Father in heaven. Amen.

fields.title: God or Mammon
fields.body_html:
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon. MATTHEW 6:24

Worldliness is one of those words that Christians use freely and define narrowly. For many in Lloyd-Jones’s generation it meant a short list of forbidden activities — the theatre, the cinema, the dance hall, the public house. The list varied from church to church, but it had one convenient feature: it usually consisted of things the speaker did not do. Lloyd-Jones would have none of it. In his exposition of Matthew 6, and in the sermon God or Mammon which can be read on Ochorus, he gave a far more searching account.

An attitude, not a list

Worldliness, he argued, is not confined to certain things. It is an attitude towards life — a general outlook that measures everything by this world and its values. It is so subtle and so pervasive that it can enter the holiest places. A man may avoid every item on the traditional list and be thoroughly worldly in his ambitions, his anxieties, his use of money, his desire for recognition. And a man may be worldly in his religion itself: in the way he seeks a reputation for spirituality, or measures his church by its size and prominence.

Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. 1 JOHN 2:15–16

He stressed, too, that our Lord’s warning in Matthew 6 is addressed to believers. It is easy to hear it as a word against the materialism of the unbelieving world. But the peculiar danger, he insisted, is to Christian people, precisely because they assume it does not apply to them.

Treasures on earth

Our Lord’s command is plain: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth.

Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. MATTHEW 6:19–20

Lloyd-Jones noted that the Lord does not merely command; He gives reasons. Earthly treasures are insecure: moth, rust and thieves take them. They capture the heart: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. They darken the understanding: if the eye is not single, the whole body is full of darkness. And they enslave: no man can serve two masters. He found in this a gracious condescension. The Lord stoops to reason with us, because the matter is so serious.

He was ready to be very practical about it. He suggested, for instance, that a Christian might test himself by his political views. If he finds that he regards one party as wholly right and the other as wholly wrong, he might ask whether his conviction really rests on principle, or on the protection of some treasure on earth he has or hopes to have. It is an uncomfortable question, and meant to be.

The single eye

The heart of the passage, for Lloyd-Jones, was the connection our Lord draws between the heart, the mind and the will. What a man treasures governs what he loves; what he loves governs what he sees; and what he sees governs how he lives.

The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. MATTHEW 6:22

He described how worldliness blinds. A man whose heart is set on earthly things begins to see everything in their light. His judgment becomes distorted. He finds reasons for doing what he wants to do. He does not notice that he is being mastered. And so the danger is not only that he will waste his life on things that perish, but that he will come to be unable to see what he is doing.

A totalitarian claim

The final verse, Ye cannot serve God and mammon, he took as a statement of God’s absolute claim. God does not ask for a share of our lives. He asks for all of them. Mammon — wealth, possessions, the things of this world personified as a rival master — asks for the same. A man cannot give himself wholly to both. He must choose.

Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. MATTHEW 6:33

In the sermon, Lloyd-Jones tells a homely story of a farmer who promised to give one of his calves to the Lord, and how, when a calf died, it turned out always to have been the Lord’s one. The point needs no story to make it. When money grows tight, the first economy most of us make is in what we give to God. The things we truly love are the last to go. That, he said, is where our real master is revealed.

The positive remedy

It would be wrong to leave Lloyd-Jones as merely a critic of worldliness. His remedy was not a new list of prohibitions but a new vision. The man who has seen the glory of God and the treasure laid up for him in heaven will find that the world loses its grip without a struggle. It is not that he forces himself to despise the world; it is that he has found something better.

Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. COLOSSIANS 3:2

Where care is needed

Lloyd-Jones’s strictures can be applied in a spirit of suspicion that makes every enjoyment of God’s good gifts seem a sin. That was not his intention. He believed that all things are the Christian’s in Christ, as the previous chapters have shown, and that the problem is not the gifts but their mastery over us. The reader should also note that his remark about political allegiance was a test of motive, not an argument for indifference to public affairs. The question is always the same: who is master?

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down what you would most hate to lose. Ask honestly whether it has become a treasure on earth.

2. Review your giving over the past year. When money was tight, what did you cut first?

3. Test your strongest opinions — political, social, professional — by asking what you might be protecting.

4. Identify one way in which worldliness may have entered your religious life: in a desire for recognition, influence or success.
