fields.body_html:
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance. PSALM 42:5

In the mid-1950s Lloyd-Jones preached a series of sermons at Westminster Chapel on a subject few preachers of his day would have touched. They were published in 1965 as Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure, and the book has become, by a wide margin, his most popular. It is not hard to see why. It deals with a condition that many Christians know from the inside and few talk about: the believer who is miserable, joyless, defeated, cast down — and who suspects, in addition to everything else, that he ought not to be.

An unhappy Christian is a poor advertisement

He began with a conviction that sounds almost harsh, but was meant as the opposite. The Christian ought to be a happy person. The New Testament is full of joy, and so was the early church. A miserable Christian is a poor advertisement for the faith, and he is also, in a real sense, dishonouring his Lord. That is not a reason for pretending to be happy. It is a reason for taking the condition seriously and seeking a cure.

Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. PHILIPPIANS 4:4

He was clear that spiritual depression is not the same as ordinary sadness, grief or suffering. The Christian weeps with those who weep, feels the pain of loss, is burdened by the sin of the world. Joy in the New Testament sense is compatible with all of that. What he had in mind was a settled condition of dejection and defeat, in which the believer has lost the sense of his privileges and lives far below them.

The doctor takes the history

It is in this book that his medical training is most visible. He did not offer a single remedy for all cases. He took the history. What kind of person are you? What has happened to you? What do you believe? The causes of spiritual depression, he held, are many, and the treatment depends on the diagnosis.

Some causes lie in temperament. Some Christians are by nature introspective, prone to self-examination to the point of morbidity; others are volatile, up one day and down the next. Grace does not abolish temperament. The same Holy Spirit works through Peter and John, and they remain recognisably themselves. A Christian must understand his own temperament, so that he is not surprised by its weaknesses.

Some causes are physical. Here the physician in him was emphatic. Tiredness, illness, overwork, the aftermath of great strain — these can bring a man low in spirit, and it is folly to treat as a spiritual problem what is really a matter of the body. He pointed to Elijah under the juniper tree, exhausted after Carmel, and to the gentleness with which God first gave him food and sleep before He dealt with him.

And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat. 1 KINGS 19:5

Some causes are spiritual, and these occupied most of his attention. He treated in turn the Christian who has never clearly grasped justification by faith and is still, in his heart, trying to earn his standing; the Christian who is tormented by his past sins and cannot believe they are really forgiven; the Christian paralysed by fear of the future; the Christian who has made his feelings the measure of his spiritual state; and the Christian who has grown weary in well-doing. He also dealt with trials, with the Lord’s chastening, and with the direct assault of the devil, who is always eager to rob the believer of his joy.

Looking back

One of the most common causes, he found, is the inability to let go of the past. Some Christians are haunted by the sins they committed before conversion; others by the wasted years; others by the thought of what might have been. He called them to Paul’s example, which is all the more striking given what Paul had once been.

Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 3:13–14

To go on grieving over sins that God has forgiven, he argued in effect, is not humility but unbelief. It treats the blood of Christ as insufficient. God has cast those sins behind His back; the believer must not keep picking them up.

Feelings

Another cause he treated at length is the tyranny of feelings. Many Christians judge their standing with God by how they feel on a given day. When they feel warm, they are sure of God’s love; when they feel cold, they doubt it. Lloyd-Jones pointed out that feelings are the most changeable thing about us, affected by weather, health and circumstance. To build the Christian life on them is to build on sand. The believer must learn to stand on the facts of what God has said and done, and let feelings follow in their own time.

For we walk by faith, not by sight. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:7

This does not mean feelings do not matter. He believed joy is a proper part of the Christian life and should be sought. But it is the fruit, not the root.

Where care is needed

This book has helped a great many people, and it can be misused. A reader suffering from severe clinical depression may hear in it a suggestion that his illness is a spiritual failure, and be crushed. That was emphatically not Lloyd-Jones’s view; he insisted on the physical factors and would have sent such a person to a doctor. His book addresses the Christian whose depression is chiefly spiritual in origin. It is not a substitute for medical care, and anyone reading it in a dark place should read it alongside proper help, and not alone.

The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. PSALM 34:18
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask honestly whether you are living far below your privileges as a Christian. What has robbed you of your joy?

2. Take your own spiritual history as a doctor would. Consider temperament, body, circumstances and belief. Where does the trouble lie?

3. If you are exhausted, attend to your body first: rest, eat, sleep. Then pray.

4. Name one past sin that you keep revisiting even though you have confessed it. Read Philippians 3:13–14 and Micah 7:19, and leave it there.

5. If your low spirits have lasted long or are severe, speak to a doctor as well as to a pastor. There is no shame in either.

A PRAYER
Lord, my soul has been cast down, and I have not always known why. Search me, and show me the cause.
Where the trouble is in my body, give me rest and wisdom to seek help. Where it is in my mind, correct my thinking by Your truth.
Deliver me from the tyranny of my feelings and from the grip of my past. Let me stand on what You have said and done.
Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, that I may praise You again for the help of Your countenance. Amen.

fields.title: Talking to Yourself
fields.body_html:
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 42:11

Of everything Lloyd-Jones taught about spiritual depression, one counsel has travelled furthest. It comes from the opening sermon of Spiritual Depression, and it is drawn from the psalm he took as his text. He is remembered above all for the insistence that the troubled Christian must learn to stop listening to himself and start talking to himself. Put so briefly, it can sound like a slogan. As he developed it, it is one of the most practical pieces of spiritual counsel of the twentieth century.

The psalmist’s method

He began by noticing what the psalmist actually does. The man is in trouble. He is far from the house of God, taunted by enemies, overwhelmed by sorrow, his tears his meat day and night. And in the middle of this he does something unexpected. He turns and addresses himself. Why art thou cast down, O my soul?

My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God? PSALM 42:3

The psalmist, Lloyd-Jones observed in effect, does not simply let his soul talk to him. He talks to his soul. He does not allow his feelings to dictate to him; he takes them in hand. He questions them, rebukes them, and directs them to God. The refrain occurs three times across Psalms 42 and 43, and each time it is the same movement: from self-pity to self-examination to hope.

Listening to yourself

The trouble with most of us, Lloyd-Jones argued, is that we listen to ourselves. We wake in the morning, and before we have done anything our thoughts begin to speak. They remind us of yesterday’s failures and today’s difficulties. They tell us that we are tired, that nothing will go right, that God has forgotten us. And we listen. We accept what they say as if it were the truth, and we allow them to set the tone of the whole day.

He did not think this was harmless. Much of the unhappiness of Christian people, he believed, comes from this passive surrender to their own moods. The self that speaks to us in this way is not a neutral reporter. It is fallen, it is affected by the body and by circumstance, and it is liable to be exploited by the devil. To listen to it uncritically is to hand the government of our lives to our weakest part.

Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. PROVERBS 4:23

Talking to yourself

The remedy is to reverse the process. Instead of letting the self talk to us, we must talk to the self. Lloyd-Jones described this as a deliberate act of the mind and will. The Christian must take himself in hand, address himself as the psalmist did, and ask: Why are you cast down? What reason do you have? And then he must preach to himself.

What does he preach? He reminds himself of God: who God is, what He has done, what He has promised. He reminds himself of what he is in Christ. He recites the facts of the gospel, against which the feelings of the moment have no standing. And he commands his soul: hope thou in God.

This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. LAMENTATIONS 3:21–22

Notice the phrase recall to my mind. Jeremiah, in the depths of his lamentation, does not wait for his feelings to change. He deliberately brings something to mind, and hope follows. That is the method exactly.

Not self-help

It would be easy to mistake this for a technique of positive thinking, and Lloyd-Jones was careful to distinguish it. The Christian is not simply telling himself that things will be better, or repeating comforting phrases. He is reminding himself of objective truth — of God and His Word — and bringing his mind into line with it. The power lies not in the talking but in the truth that is spoken. Without the facts of the gospel, talking to oneself is merely whistling in the dark.

Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. ISAIAH 26:3

Nor did he think it was easy. It requires discipline, and the discipline must be practised before the crisis comes. The Christian who has stored his mind with Scripture will have something to say to himself when the dark day arrives. The one who has not will have only his feelings.

The place of the mind

This counsel grows directly out of one of Lloyd-Jones’s deepest convictions: that the Christian life engages the whole person, and that the mind has a leading place. God speaks to us through truth, and truth is received first by the understanding. He was suspicious of any form of Christianity that bypassed the mind and appealed directly to the emotions or the will. Emotions stirred without truth soon fade. The will pressed without truth soon breaks. But truth understood and believed warms the heart and moves the will.

Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. ROMANS 12:2

This is why he was so often called a preacher to the mind, though that description is incomplete. He addressed the mind because he believed that is the door through which God ordinarily comes to the heart.

Where care is needed

There is a danger that this counsel, applied without wisdom, becomes another burden: the depressed person, already struggling, is told that the problem is simply that he has not talked to himself properly. Lloyd-Jones did not intend it that way. As the previous chapter showed, he took the physical and temperamental causes of depression seriously, and knew that some conditions need a doctor. Talking to yourself is a medicine for the soul; it does not replace medicine for the body. It is also best practised in company. The psalmist spoke to himself, but he also longed for the house of God and the voice of joy among the multitude. The Christian who is cast down needs both his own preaching and the fellowship of the church.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Notice what your thoughts say to you in the first ten minutes of tomorrow. Write it down.

2. Then answer it. Speak to your soul as the psalmist did, with specific truths from Scripture.

3. Choose three passages of Scripture to learn by heart this month, so that you have something to say to yourself on a dark day.

4. Read Psalms 42 and 43 aloud, and notice the movement of the refrain each time it comes.

5. If you know someone who is cast down, do not only listen to them; gently remind them of what God has said.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have listened to myself too long. I have let my moods and fears speak, and I have believed them.
Teach me to take myself in hand, to question my soul, and to preach Your truth to my own heart.
Stay my mind on You, and keep me in perfect peace. Let me recall Your mercies, and so have hope.
And when I cannot speak to myself, send me brothers and sisters who will speak Your Word to me. Amen.

fields.title: Work Out Your Own Salvation
fields.body_html:
Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. PHILIPPIANS 2:12–13

Lloyd-Jones preached through the Epistle to the Philippians in the years after the war, and the sermons were later gathered in two volumes, The Life of Joy and The Life of Peace. One of those sermons, on working out our salvation, can be read on Ochorus. It gives his teaching on the Christian life in its most compact form, and it answers a question every believer must face sooner or later: if salvation is all of grace, what part do I play?

Doctrine first, then therefore

He began, as he often did, by drawing attention to a single word: wherefore. Paul’s appeal for Christian conduct does not come out of the blue. It follows from what he has just said about Christ, who humbled Himself and became obedient to death and was highly exalted. The pattern, Lloyd-Jones observed, runs through every New Testament epistle. Doctrine comes first. Then comes a therefore or a wherefore. Then the appeal for conduct.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

This, for him, was the fundamental difference between Christianity and every merely ethical system. The world tells a man how to live and then leaves him to it. The New Testament first tells him what God has done for him, and then says, in effect: if you believe that, can you not see that this must follow? The appeal is to reason, to equity, to fair play. It is not law but the perfect law of liberty.

He drew from this a searching test. How do we react when the gospel calls us to live in a particular way? If we enjoy hearing about grace but bristle when it calls for self-denial, something is wrong not only with our conduct but with our grasp of the doctrine. For the two cannot be separated.

What working out does not mean

He was careful first to say what Paul does not mean. He does not mean work for your salvation, as though a man could earn his standing before God. Philippians itself, in its third chapter, is one of the clearest statements in Scripture that righteousness is not by works but through the faith of Christ. The believer already has salvation. He is not working towards it; he is working it out.

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

Working out means carrying through to completion something already given. The salvation that God has planted must come to expression in the whole of life. The believer is to apply it, develop it, bring it to bear on every area of his conduct.

With fear and trembling

How is this to be done? Paul says: with fear and trembling. Lloyd-Jones insisted this does not mean with craven terror or anxious uncertainty. It means with reverence, with seriousness, with a sense of the greatness of the matter and of our own weakness. It is the opposite of casualness. The Christian who treats holiness lightly has not understood the cost at which he was saved.

And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man’s work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear. 1 PETER 1:17

He was sharply critical of any teaching that made sanctification passive — that told believers simply to let go and let God, to wait for a crisis experience that would lift them above the struggle. That is not what Paul says. Paul says work. The New Testament is full of exhortations to effort: mortify, put off, put on, flee, follow, fight. The Christian is not a spectator of his own sanctification.

For it is God

But Paul immediately adds the great ground of encouragement: for it is God which worketh in you. The believer works because God works. His effort is not independent of grace but the fruit of it. God works in him both to will and to do: He gives the desire and the power alike.

Lloyd-Jones found in this the answer both to despair and to pride. The Christian need not despair, because he is not alone; the Almighty is at work in him. And he cannot be proud, because even his willing is God’s gift.

Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

If we will not

The sermon on Ochorus ends on a sober note, and it is worth hearing. God will bring His people to perfection. If they respond to His promptings and give themselves to the work, well. If they do not, He loves them too much to leave them as they are, and He may use other means — chastening, disappointment, illness, loss. Lloyd-Jones was careful to say that not all suffering is chastening. But he believed that some is, and that the Christian who neglects his sanctification should not be surprised if God takes it in hand Himself.

For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. HEBREWS 12:6

Where care is needed

The warning about chastening must be handled gently. It is not a key for interpreting every hardship in another person’s life, and it should never be used to wound someone who is already suffering. Lloyd-Jones himself qualified it carefully. It is a word for our own consciences, not for our neighbour’s. The heart of this chapter is not the warning but the promise: God is at work in you, and He will finish what He began.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read any New Testament epistle and find the point where doctrine turns to therefore. Notice how the appeal grows out of what came before.

2. Ask how you react when Scripture calls you to self-denial. Does it reveal anything about your grasp of grace?

3. Identify one area of your life where you have been passive about holiness, waiting for change rather than working it out. Take one concrete step this week.

4. When you are tempted to pride in your spiritual progress, remember who gave you both the will and the power.

5. Consider whether any present difficulty might be God’s loving discipline. Ask Him humbly, and do not press the question on others.

A PRAYER
Father, You have saved me by grace, and You have called me to work out that salvation in every part of my life.
Forgive me for loving the doctrine and resisting its demands. Let every therefore in Your Word find me willing.
Work in me both to will and to do of Your good pleasure. Give me the desire, and give me the strength.
And if I will not follow Your promptings, love me enough to chasten me, until I am made like Your Son. Amen.

fields.title: Joy Unspeakable
fields.body_html:
Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 PETER 1:8

This chapter deals with the most distinctive, and the most debated, part of Lloyd-Jones’s teaching. He believed that there is an experience of the Holy Spirit, which the New Testament calls the baptism with the Spirit, that is distinct from conversion; that it brings the believer an overwhelming assurance of God’s love and a new power for witness; and that many Christians have never known it and should seek it. Some of his closest friends in the Reformed world disagreed with him, and the disagreement continues. The aim here is to set out what he taught as fairly as possible, and then the objections, as fairly.

Where he taught it

He taught it in several places: in his expositions of Romans 8 and of Ephesians 1, and above all in a series of sermons on John’s Gospel preached in the mid-1960s and published after his death as Joy Unspeakable, with a companion volume, Prove All Things, on the gifts. He had held the view in some form for many years; it was not an innovation of old age. And it was closely tied to his longing for revival, which is the subject of the next chapter.

What he taught

His argument ran broadly like this. In the New Testament, the Holy Spirit does many things. He regenerates — gives new life to those who were dead. Every Christian has experienced that, or he is not a Christian at all. He indwells every believer. He leads, sanctifies and helps. All of this is the common possession of the whole church.

Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. ROMANS 8:9

But the New Testament also speaks of the Spirit coming upon believers in a way that is evident and powerful. The disciples were already believers before Pentecost, yet they were told to wait for power from on high. The Samaritans in Acts 8 believed and were baptised, and only afterwards received the Spirit. The Ephesian disciples in Acts 19 were asked whether they had received the Holy Ghost since they believed.

Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? ACTS 19:2

From passages like these, Lloyd-Jones concluded that the baptism with the Spirit is not simply another name for regeneration. It is a distinct experience, which may come at conversion or later, and which may be repeated. Its chief mark, as he understood it, is assurance — a direct and overwhelming witness of the Spirit that the believer is a child of God, going beyond the inference he draws from Scripture and from the evidence of his own life.

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. ROMANS 8:16

He identified this with Paul’s language of sealing in Ephesians 1:13, and with the joy unspeakable and full of glory of which Peter speaks. And he believed that it had been the experience of many of the great figures of church history — he pointed to men such as the Puritan Thomas Goodwin, to the leaders of the eighteenth-century awakening, and to preachers of the Welsh revivals — who testified to a moment or season when the love of God was poured into their hearts in a way that transformed them and their ministry.

In whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise. EPHESIANS 1:13

Why it mattered to him

He was driven by a pastoral and a historical concern. Pastorally, he saw a church that was orthodox and dry — correct in its doctrine but lacking joy, assurance and power. He believed that an evangelicalism which said, in effect, that every believer has already received everything at conversion and need seek nothing more, had closed the door to what the church most needed. Historically, he saw that the great eras of the church had been marked by a vivid experience of the Spirit, and he feared that the evangelicals of his day had, by their definitions, ruled out any expectation of such a thing.

How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13

He was also careful. He warned against seeking experiences for their own sake, against manufactured emotion, and against any method that promised the Spirit on demand. The baptism with the Spirit, as he taught it, is sovereignly given by Christ, not produced by human technique. On the gifts, he refused to say that they had ceased, but he was also cautious about the claims of the charismatic movement then emerging, and insisted that all things be tested by Scripture.

The objections

Many who loved and admired him could not follow him here. John Stott, in a short book on the baptism and fullness of the Spirit, argued that the New Testament presents the baptism with the Spirit as the initial blessing every Christian receives at conversion, and that the later experiences Christians may have are better described as being filled with the Spirit, which is repeatable and commanded of all. Others in his own Reformed tradition — J. I. Packer among them — shared his longing for a deeper experience of God but questioned his exegesis, and worried that a two-stage doctrine could divide Christians into haves and have-nots and encourage an unhealthy seeking after experience. Some felt that his teaching, whatever his intentions, opened a door to charismatic practices he himself did not endorse.

These are serious objections from serious people. It is fair to say that most Reformed evangelicals today side with Stott and Packer on the exegesis, while many share Lloyd-Jones’s concern that the church should expect more of the Spirit than it commonly does.

What can be received from him

Whatever one concludes about the terminology, his burden is plainly scriptural. The New Testament does speak of a joy that is unspeakable, of the love of God shed abroad in the heart, of the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit. These are meant to be real in experience, not merely held as doctrine. A Christian who has never known them should not assume that this is all there is. He should ask.

And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. ROMANS 5:5
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Acts 2, 8 and 19. Note what happens to believers in each and form your own judgment from the text.

2. Ask whether your Christianity is marked by joy and assurance, or only by correct belief. Be honest.

3. If you have strong views on this question either way, read a careful statement of the other view before you speak about it again.

4. Pray Luke 11:13 for yourself this week, asking your heavenly Father for a fuller experience of His Spirit, without prescribing the form it must take.

5. Guard against despising believers whose experience of the Spirit differs from yours, in either direction.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, You gave me life when I was dead. Thank You that You dwell in me and that I am Christ’s.
Forgive me for being content with a dry orthodoxy. Shed abroad the love of God in my heart, and bear witness with my spirit that I am His child.
Guard me from seeking experiences for their own sake, and from judging others by mine.
Give me joy unspeakable and full of glory, and power to witness to Christ, for His name’s sake. Amen.

fields.title: Revival
fields.body_html:
O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy. HABAKKUK 3:2

Lloyd-Jones grew up in the shadow of revival. Llangeitho, the village of his boyhood, had been one of the centres of the great eighteenth-century awakening in Wales under Daniel Rowland. His wife’s grandfather had been a preacher of the Welsh revivals of the following century. And he was a small boy when the revival of 1904 and 1905 swept through Wales. He read the history of revivals all his life, and he prayed for revival all his life. In 1959, the centenary of the great revival of 1859 in Wales, Ulster and America, he preached a series of sermons on the subject at Westminster Chapel, afterwards published simply as Revival. A shorter address, What Is Revival?, can be read on Ochorus.

What revival is

He began, characteristically, with a definition. Revival, he said, is a period of unusual blessing and activity in the life of the Christian church. It happens first to the church, to believing people, and only in consequence to those outside. That definition, he argued, clears away a great confusion. A revival is not the same thing as an evangelistic campaign.

An evangelistic campaign, as he put it in effect, is the church deciding to do something for those outside. A revival is something done to the church. It is not organised, advertised or produced. It comes down from heaven. The church does not decide to have one; it is visited.

And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. ACTS 2:2

He described it as, in a sense, a repetition of the day of Pentecost: the Holy Spirit coming down upon a number of people together — a church, a district, sometimes a whole country — so that they become aware of His presence and power as never before.

The marks of revival

He found the same features in every revival he had read about. The first is an overwhelming awareness of the glory and holiness of God. Things that people had heard a thousand times suddenly become vivid, luminous and unmistakably real. They are filled with awe. There is little lightness in a true revival, he observed, and no need of organisation to produce an effect; there is instead a holy fear.

Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. ISAIAH 6:5

The second, flowing from the first, is a deep conviction of sin. People who had thought themselves respectable see themselves as vile and helpless, and may be held in that distress for days or weeks. The third is a clear sight of the love of God in Christ, and a joy that follows the conviction. The fourth is an outflow to the world: those outside the church, who had been deaf to every appeal, find themselves compelled to listen. Communities are changed. Numbers are added. But the numbers are the fruit, not the root.

Why he distrusted technique

His understanding of revival shaped his attitude to much of the evangelism of his day. He was deeply wary of methods that aimed to produce results by human means — mass campaigns, emotional pressure, appeals to come forward. He did not doubt that some were genuinely converted in such settings. But he feared that the church had come to believe it could do by organisation what only God can do by His Spirit, and that it was mistaking its own activity for the work of God.

Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. ZECHARIAH 4:6

This conviction gave his ministry its particular character. He did not try to build a large church by methods. He preached, and he prayed, and he waited on God. He believed that the greatest need of the church was not more activity but a visitation from heaven.

Praying for revival

If revival cannot be organised, what can the church do? Lloyd-Jones’s answer was: pray. He pointed to the pattern of Scripture, where revival is so often preceded by God’s people crying out to Him in their need. And he urged the church to pray for it with urgency and with expectation.

Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence. ISAIAH 64:1

But he added a note that must not be missed. The motive for praying for revival must be the glory of God, not the excitement of the church. We are not to seek it for the experience, or the sensation, or the numbers, but that His great name may be known and magnified among the people. The address on Ochorus closes on exactly that note.

Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee? PSALM 85:6

Sovereign and yet sought

There is an apparent tension here, and Lloyd-Jones embraced it. Revival is sovereign: God sends it when and where He will, and no one can command it. And yet revival is to be sought: God’s people are to pray for it, prepare for it and long for it. He did not think these were contradictory. fields.body_html:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. 2 TIMOTHY 4:2

In the spring of 1969, a year after he left Westminster Chapel, Lloyd-Jones gave a series of lectures to students at Westminster Theological Seminary in Philadelphia. They were published in 1971 as Preaching and Preachers, and the book has shaped more preachers, in more countries, than perhaps any other written in the twentieth century. It is also the book in which he is most personal. He wrote as a man who had given up medicine for the pulpit and had never once regretted it.

The highest calling

He opened with a bold claim. Nothing, he argued, is a higher calling than preaching, and nothing is more urgently needed by the church in any age. He did not say this to exalt preachers. He said it because of what preaching is: God’s appointed means of bringing His Word to bear upon men and women, for their salvation and their building up.

For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:21

He was writing against the tide. In the 1960s many were saying that the age of preaching was over. People would no longer sit and listen to a man speak; the church must turn to discussion, drama, counselling, social action, film. Lloyd-Jones would have none of it. He did not deny that these things have their place. But he insisted that nothing can replace preaching, and that a church which relegates it has lost its way. The decline of preaching, he believed, was not the cause of the church’s weakness but a symptom of it — a symptom of lost confidence in the Word of God.

What preaching is

What is preaching? He is remembered for the phrase logic on fire, and the phrase sums up his view. Preaching is not merely a lecture, however learned, nor merely an emotional appeal, however moving. It is sound doctrine set ablaze in the man who delivers it. It must have logic: clear thought, sound doctrine, careful exposition, an argument that the mind can follow. And it must have fire: the preacher must be gripped by the truth he preaches, and it must come from him with urgency, warmth and power.

Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures? LUKE 24:32

He insisted on both halves. A preacher who has logic without fire gives lectures; the congregation may be instructed but will not be moved. A preacher who has fire without logic stirs the emotions but leaves nothing solid behind. The true preacher reasons and burns at once.

The preacher and the sermon

He had much practical counsel. The preacher must be called; a man should enter the ministry only when he finds he cannot stay out of it. He must be a man of prayer and a diligent student of Scripture, reading through the whole Bible regularly, not only the passages he means to preach. He must know his people. He must prepare with great care, and yet not be so bound to his notes that the Spirit has no room to move him.

He distinguished between the sermon and preaching. The sermon is the prepared material — the exposition, the argument, the structure. Preaching is the act of delivering it, in which the whole man is involved: mind, heart, voice and body. A man may prepare an excellent sermon and fail to preach it.

And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:4

He was sharply critical of certain habits. He disliked preachers who tried to entertain, who relied on humour and anecdote, who sought to impress by eloquence or learning. He disliked the practice of reading sermons word for word from a manuscript. He was wary of appeals and techniques designed to produce an immediate response. And he had no patience with the idea that the preacher should adapt his message to what the modern mind finds acceptable.

Unction

The most important thing of all, he said, is the unction of the Holy Spirit. This is the anointing that comes upon the preacher and his words, making them living and powerful in a way that no human skill can produce. The preacher is conscious of it; so is the congregation. It is not something he can command, but he can seek it, and he must.

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me. ACTS 1:8

He urged preachers to seek this power constantly, to expect it, and to be dissatisfied without it. Without unction, the best preparation and the soundest doctrine fall flat. With it, the simplest words can pierce the heart.

The preacher as physician

Throughout, the physician is visible. The preacher, as he saw it, is dealing with souls, and the stakes are eternal. He must diagnose as well as prescribe. He must not preach over people’s heads, nor pander to them. He must apply the truth to their condition, press it home, and leave them face to face with God.

Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. COLOSSIANS 1:28

Where care is needed

Preaching and Preachers is a strong book, and strong books overstate. Lloyd-Jones could be dismissive of practices that God has used — reading manuscripts, public appeals, forms of worship other than his own — and a preacher need not follow him in every prohibition. His view that the preacher should not engage much in counselling would strike many pastors today as too narrow. And his model of long, consecutive expository series suited his gifts and his setting; not every preacher, or every congregation, is equipped for it. But the heart of the book is beyond dispute. The church needs preachers who reason and burn, who open the Scriptures and are themselves on fire, and who look to the Spirit for power. That is a standard every preacher may measure himself by.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you preach or teach, ask whether your preaching has more logic or more fire. What does it lack?

2. Pray this week, by name, for the preachers you sit under, that they may have unction from the Holy Spirit.

3. When you next listen to a sermon, pray before it begins that God will speak, and come expecting Him to.

4. If you are a preacher, read through a book of the Bible this month simply for your own soul, not for sermon preparation.

5. Ask whether you have come to value preaching less than other activities in church life. Why?

A PRAYER
Lord God, it has pleased You by the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Thank You for everyone who has opened Your Word to me.
Raise up preachers in our day who reason clearly and burn brightly, who fear You and not the opinion of men.
Give them unction from on high. Let their words come in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.
And give me a heart that burns as Your Word is opened, and a will that obeys it. Amen.

fields.title: The Church and Evangelical Unity
fields.body_html:
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. EPHESIANS 4:3

This chapter concerns the most painful episode of Lloyd-Jones’s public life, and it must be told with care. On the evening of the eighteenth of October, 1966, at the National Assembly of Evangelicals convened by the Evangelical Alliance in Westminster Central Hall, he made an appeal that has been argued over ever since. What he said, how it was answered, and what followed divided British evangelicals for a generation. Good men stood on both sides. The aim here is not to settle the dispute but to explain what he believed and why, and to set beside it the convictions of those who could not follow him.

The setting

The 1960s were the high noon of the ecumenical movement. The World Council of Churches had been founded in 1948, and in Britain there was serious talk of the major denominations coming together into a single national church within a generation. Many churches, at the same time, openly tolerated ministers and teachers who denied doctrines evangelicals regarded as essential: the deity of Christ, His atoning death, His bodily resurrection, the authority of Scripture.

Evangelicals were scattered through all these denominations — Anglican, Baptist, Congregational, Methodist, Presbyterian — usually as minorities. They cooperated across denominational lines in bodies such as the Inter-Varsity Fellowship and the Evangelical Alliance. But their primary loyalty, in church terms, was to their own denominations.

What he believed

Lloyd-Jones had been thinking about the doctrine of the church for years, and he had come to firm convictions. The church, he believed, is defined by the gospel. Unity in the New Testament is not an organisational matter but a unity of those who share the same life and the same faith. It follows that there can be no true unity with those who deny the gospel, however large and venerable the institution that holds them together.

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. JUDE 1:3

He thought that evangelicals had got things the wrong way round. They were in close institutional fellowship with people who denied the faith, and in only loose, occasional fellowship with each other. The ecumenical movement was pressing the churches towards a larger union on a doctrinally minimal basis, and he feared that evangelicals would be swept along. The time had come, he believed, for them to put the gospel before denominational loyalty.

The appeal

On that October evening he called on evangelicals to consider seriously whether they should remain in mixed denominations, and to come together in a fellowship of evangelical churches. Exactly what he intended has been debated ever since — whether a new denomination, a looser association, or simply a readiness to act together when conscience required. His admirers and his critics have read the address differently, and his biographer Iain Murray reads him more narrowly than many did at the time. What is not in doubt is that the appeal was heard by many as a call to leave their churches.

Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:17

The reply

John Stott, the rector of All Souls, Langham Place, was in the chair. At the end of the address, he rose and, departing from the ordinary role of a chairman, publicly disagreed. He said that in his judgment history and Scripture were against the view that had been expressed, and urged his hearers not to make hasty decisions. It was widely understood as a direct rebuttal. Stott later acknowledged that he had misused his position as chairman, and went to Lloyd-Jones to apologise for that, though not for his convictions. The following year, at the National Evangelical Anglican Congress at Keele, Anglican evangelicals committed themselves to remaining in the Church of England and playing a fuller part in its life.

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! PSALM 133:1

What followed

The consequences were lasting. Evangelicals in Britain were divided, broadly, into those who stayed within the mixed denominations and those who left or aligned themselves with independent evangelical groups. Old friendships were strained. Lloyd-Jones and Stott, who had admired one another, drew apart. A few years later, when J. I. Packer co-authored a book with Anglo-Catholic writers on the future of the Church of England, Lloyd-Jones felt he could no longer work with him, and the Puritan Conference that the two had led for some twenty years was brought to an end, to be succeeded by a new conference without Packer. It was, on any reckoning, a costly outcome.

Weighing it

It is tempting to make one man the hero and the other the villain, and it would be wrong. Both were godly. Both believed they were being faithful to Scripture. Both paid a price. Lloyd-Jones was surely right that doctrinal indifference is fatal to the church, and that unity without truth is no unity at all. His critics were surely right that the New Testament also calls believers to patience, to remain where they can bear faithful witness, and to be very slow to divide. Many who stayed in their denominations did so from conviction, not compromise, and saw real gains. Some who left found themselves in small and struggling fellowships. Readers of this book will belong to many different churches and will weigh the matter differently.

That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. JOHN 17:21

What can be received from Lloyd-Jones here, whatever one’s view of 1966, is his insistence that the church is defined by the gospel, and that the unity Christ prayed for is a unity in the truth. And what must be learned from the whole episode is how easily such convictions, even rightly held, can be expressed in ways that wound brothers.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. PHILIPPIANS 2:3
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what you believe defines a true church. Write it down, and test it against Scripture.

2. Consider your own church. Where is the gospel clearly held, and where might it be compromised?

3. If you have strong views on the question of separation, read a careful statement of the other side this month.

4. Think of a fellow believer with whom you have differed sharply. Pray for him or her by name, and consider whether you owe an apology for the manner, if not the substance, of your disagreement.

5. Pray for the unity of all who truly love Christ in your town or city.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You prayed that Your people might be one, and You are the truth. Keep me from a unity that sacrifices the gospel, and from a zeal for truth that forgets love.
Give wisdom to Your church in every land, to know when to stay and when to go, and grace to respect those who judge differently.
Heal the wounds that have come between Your servants, and forgive us where we have spoken in pride.
Make us one in You, that the world may believe. Amen.

Stott later acknowledged that he had misused his position as chairman, and went to Lloyd-Jones to apologise for that, though not for his convictions. The following year, at the National Evangelical Anglican Congress at Keele, Anglican evangelicals committed themselves to remaining in the Church of England and playing a fuller part in its life. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! PSALM 133:1 What followed The consequences were lasting. Evangelicals in Britain were divided, broadly, into those who stayed within the mixed denominations and those who left or aligned themselves with independent evangelical groups. Old friendships were strained. Lloyd-Jones and Stott, who had admired one another, drew apart. A few years later, when J. I. Packer co-authored a book with Anglo-Catholic writers on the future of the Church of England, Lloyd-Jones felt he could no longer work with him, and the Puritan Conference that the two had led for some twenty years was brought to an end, to be succeeded by a new conference without Packer. It was, on any reckoning, a costly outcome. Weighing it It is tempting to make one man the hero and the other the villain, and it would be wrong. Both were godly. Both believed they were being faithful to Scripture. Both paid a price. Lloyd-Jones was surely right that doctrinal indifference is fatal to the church, and that unity without truth is no unity at all. His critics were surely right that the New Testament also calls believers to patience, to remain where they can bear faithful witness, and to be very slow to divide. Many who stayed in their denominations did so from conviction, not compromise, and saw real gains. Some who left found themselves in small and struggling fellowships. Readers of this book will belong to many different churches and will weigh the matter differently. That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. JOHN 17:21 What can be received from Lloyd-Jones here, whatever one’s view of 1966, is his insistence that the church is defined by the gospel, and that the unity Christ prayed for is a unity in the truth. And what must be learned from the whole episode is how easily such convictions, even rightly held, can be expressed in ways that wound brothers. Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. PHILIPPIANS 2:3 FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Ask what you believe defines a true church. Write it down, and test it against Scripture. 2. Consider your own church. Where is the gospel clearly held, and where might it be compromised? 3. If you have strong views on the question of separation, read a careful statement of the other side this month. 4. Think of a fellow believer with whom you have differed sharply. Pray for him or her by name, and consider whether you owe an apology for the manner, if not the substance, of your disagreement. 5. Pray for the unity of all who truly love Christ in your town or city. A PRAYER Lord Jesus, You prayed that Your people might be one, and You are the truth. Keep me from a unity that sacrifices the gospel, and from a zeal for truth that forgets love. Give wisdom to Your church in every land, to know when to stay and when to go, and grace to respect those who judge differently. Heal the wounds that have come between Your servants, and forgive us where we have spoken in pride. Make us one in You, that the world may believe. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. MATTHEW 9:12

We have covered a good deal of ground in seventeen short chapters, and it would be easy to come away with the impression that Martyn Lloyd-Jones taught many things. He did. He preached for more than fifty years, and he rarely preached on a text without taking it apart word by word. But in truth, like every great physician, he was concerned with one thing. He wanted to know what was really wrong with people, and he wanted to bring them to the only cure.

The diagnosis and the cure

Look back over the chapters and the pattern is plain. The doctor’s method, in chapter three, was the key to all the rest. The plight of man in Ephesians 2 was his diagnosis: dead in sins, walking according to the course of this world, by nature children of wrath. The sovereignty of God, justification by faith, the cross and union with Christ were the cure — God’s free and total remedy for a disease man could not touch. The Sermon on the Mount showed what the cured patient looks like: poor in spirit, meek, hungry for righteousness, salt and light in a corrupting world. Spiritual depression was his treatment of the patient who has been cured and does not feel it. And his teaching on the Spirit, on revival and on preaching all sprang from the conviction that the remedy is not a technique but the living God Himself, acting by His Word and Spirit.

But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) EPHESIANS 2:4–5

If this book has done its work, the reader will not come away chiefly admiring the Doctor. He will come away having been examined — and, if he has been honest, having found in himself the disease the Doctor spent his life describing, and having gone to the Physician who alone can heal it.

What to do with it

Lloyd-Jones believed that truth which is merely understood has not yet done its work. It must be applied, felt and obeyed. So here is the plainest counsel this book can give.

Go back to the chapter that searched you most. Not the one you found most interesting or agreed with most readily, but the one that touched a nerve. That is probably where God is dealing with you. Take the questions at the end of it, and work through them slowly, over weeks rather than days. Then go on to the next.

Learn to talk to yourself. Of all his counsels, this is perhaps the most immediately useful. When your moods speak, do not simply listen. Answer them with what God has said.

Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 43:5

And go to the Word. Lloyd-Jones would be dismayed to think that anyone had read a book about him instead of reading the Bible. His whole ministry was an attempt to get people to open the Scriptures and hear God speak. Read slowly, read whole books, and ask of every passage what it says, why, and what it requires of you.

A word about the man

We have been honest in these pages about the places where Lloyd-Jones must be read with care. His call of 1966 divided brethren who should have stood together, and the costs were real. His teaching on the baptism with the Spirit was disputed by some of his closest friends, and most Reformed interpreters today do not follow his exegesis. His criticisms of the church life and evangelism of his day could be sweeping, and he was not always generous to methods he distrusted. His long series and severe manner did not suit everyone.

None of this has been said to diminish him. It has been said because he himself taught that no preacher is to be followed blindly, that every man’s teaching must be tested by the Word of God, and that the servant is nothing and the Master everything. He would have been uncomfortable with a book that made him its hero.

For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:5

What remains, when the controversies have been weighed, is a man who gave up one of the most enviable careers in Britain because he had become convinced of what was really wrong with people, and who spent the rest of his life offering them the one remedy he trusted. He believed that the deepest trouble in every human heart is curable. He believed it because he had found the cure himself.

The last word

The last word belongs not to him but to the Lord he preached. The gospel Lloyd-Jones preached for half a century was not his message but Christ’s, and it is addressed now to the reader of this book as directly as it was to the congregations at Sandfields and Westminster.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. MATTHEW 11:28

The Doctor has done his work if he has sent you to the Physician.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look back over the chapter titles and choose the one that searched you most. Return to it this week and do its application points slowly.

2. Write down, in a few sentences, the diagnosis of your own soul as Scripture gives it — and then the cure.

3. Practise talking to yourself every morning this week, answering your moods with specific promises of God.

4. Choose one of Lloyd-Jones’s books named in the Reader’s Guide, obtain it from its publisher, and read it slowly with your Bible open.

5. Pray for the preachers and churches of your land, that God would visit them again.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, Great Physician, You have shown me my disease, and You have not left me in it. You are the cure.
Do not let me admire the doctor and neglect the medicine. Do not let me become a student of the gospel instead of a partaker of it.
Search me, humble me, and bring me again and again to Your cross.
And when I am cast down, teach me to preach Your truth to my own soul, and to hope in You. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Martyn Lloyd-Jones
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Lloyd-Jones wrote very few books as books. Almost everything that bears his name began as preaching — Sunday sermons, Friday-evening expositions, conference addresses and lectures — taken down, edited and published, many of them after his death. There is a great deal of it, and much of it is long. The guide below is arranged to help the reader find a way in. His works remain in copyright and should be obtained from their publishers; none is reproduced in this book.

Begin here

Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure (1965). His best-loved book, and the one most likely to help a struggling believer. Short chapters, each on a single cause, with the doctor’s care for diagnosis on every page. The source of chapters thirteen and fourteen of this volume.

Studies in the Sermon on the Mount. Two volumes, published at the end of the 1950s. Practical, searching and accessible, and perhaps the best introduction to his preaching. The source of chapters ten to twelve. Several of these sermons can be read on Ochorus.

The Cross. A short series on Galatians 6:14. An excellent single evening’s reading, and a good test of whether his style suits you.

The great expository series

Romans. Fourteen volumes from the Friday-evening series at Westminster Chapel, covering the epistle from the first chapter into the fourteenth. The volumes on chapters three to six — Atonement and Justification, Assurance and The New Man — are the heart of it. Demanding and rewarding.

Ephesians. Eight volumes from the Sunday-morning series. God’s Way of Reconciliation, on chapter two, is the place to start. The last volumes, on spiritual warfare, are among his most practical.

Life in Christ. His sermons on the First Epistle of John, on fellowship with God, assurance and love.

The Life of Joy and The Life of Peace. Sermons on Philippians, warm and pastoral. One of them can be read on Ochorus.

On preaching

Preaching and Preachers (1971). Lectures given in Philadelphia in 1969. Indispensable for anyone who preaches or teaches, and illuminating for anyone who listens. Strong opinions throughout; weigh them.

On the Spirit and revival

Revival. Sermons preached in 1959, the centenary of the 1859 revival. His fullest statement of what revival is and why the church should pray for it. A short address on the same subject can be read on Ochorus.

Joy Unspeakable and Prove All Things. His teaching on the baptism with the Spirit and on spiritual gifts, published after his death. Read with the cautions in chapter sixteen of this volume, and alongside John Stott’s short book on the baptism and fullness of the Holy Spirit, which argues the other side.

Doctrine and the church

Great Doctrines of the Bible. Lectures on systematic theology given on Friday evenings in the early 1950s, now usually published in one volume. Clear and orderly.

Authority. A short book on the authority of Christ, Scripture and the Spirit.

Knowing the Times. Addresses on various occasions, including material related to the controversy of 1966. Read with chapter nineteen of this volume in mind.

About Lloyd-Jones

Iain H. Murray’s two-volume biography, D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones: The First Forty Years and The Fight of Faith, is the standard life, written by a close colleague who had access to his papers. It is detailed, admiring and indispensable, though readers who disagree with Lloyd-Jones on 1966 will find its account partisan. Bethan Lloyd-Jones’s Memories of Sandfields gives a vivid picture of the early ministry. For a more critical assessment, the academic studies of his place in twentieth-century evangelicalism, such as that by John Brencher, are worth reading alongside Murray. No single account is disinterested; reading more than one is wise. The Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography.

On Ochorus

A number of his sermons can be read in the Ochorus library, among them The Salt of the Earth, The Light of the World, God or Mammon, Jesus on Prayer, The Wrath of God, The Parable of the Prodigal Son, What Is Revival?, Working Out Our Own Salvation, So Great Salvation, Full Salvation and A Living Hope of the Hereafter. They are the best place to hear his own voice.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. He would have insisted on it. His method was to take a text and press it; check the text.

Read him slowly. His sermons were meant to be heard one a week, not devoured in a sitting. A single sermon read carefully and prayed over will do more good than a volume skimmed.

Read him for the diagnosis and the cure. Where he presses a controversial point, weigh it. But do not let the controversies distract you from the thing he cared about most: your own condition before God, and the remedy God has provided in Christ.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
